newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Historic Vietnam War meet sets course for failure.
newsitem.headline: Historic Vietnam War meet sets course for failure.

text.p: Former leading foes from the United States and Vietnam sat down together in Hanoi on Friday to discuss missed opportunities from the Vietnam War, but even as the historic meeting began it appeared doomed.

As the conference got under way senior U.S. delegates, including former U.S. defence chief Robert McNamara, spoke to reporters of a mission to heal wounds and help future generations by learning lessons from history.

But in a sign of the continuing mindset gulf between the world's most powerful nation and one of its poorest, Vietnamese officials made clear that if there were lessons to be learnt, they were not for Vietnam.
"We'll be looking at 10 missed opportunities for the United States," Luu Van Loi, a retired diplomat and member of the negotiating team at the 1972 Paris peace talks, told Reuters.
"There were no missed opportunities for Vietnam. We had no option but to fight. If we didn't fight we would have been beaten."
Ambassador Dao Huy Ngoc, General Director of Vietnam's Institute for International Relations and chairman at the conference, was similarly direct.
"We will be talking about whether there were missed opportunities for both sides," he said. "Anyway, Vietnam affirms that we did not miss any."

The Vietnam War ended in April 1975 with the climactic fall of U.S.-backed Saigon to the forces of communist North Vietnam, three years after the United States had negotiated a withdrawal of its military forces from the country.
The immediate cost in human lives for the United States was 58,000 dead and for Vietnam some three million.

In subsequent memoirs recounting his involvement in the critical years of the conflict between 1962 and 1968, Robert McNamara spoke of United States policymakers having been "wrong, terribly wrong" to escalate America's involvement in a war where it was destined to fail.

McNamara proposed a series of topics for discussion at this week's meeting. Those included the failure of negotiation initiatives between 1965 and 1968, the possibility for a U.S. withdrawal in September 1967, and the prospects for a U.S. victory or war with China or the Soviet Union if Washington had opted for an even bigger military campaign.
Speaking to reporters, however, he maintained there had been missed opportunities for Hanoi as well as Washington and that these should be discussed.
"You heard the ambassador (Dao Huy Ngoc) refer this morning to missed opportunities," he said. "He didn't say only the U.S., but presumably Vietnam and the U.S."
"Each missed opportunities to avoid this tragic loss of life."

The conference is scheduled to run until Monday and comes just days before a visit by U.S. State Secretary Madeleine Albright. She is scheduled to discuss a range of issues with Hanoi including human rights and the search for missing American servicemen.
